For a while (2018-2022) it was hot to buy up software companies that dominated a single niche and jack up prices. The bet was that since software is such a 0-1 business that they would have great moats and have strong pricing power. My father-in-law is blind and used to use JAWS until it got bought up by a private equity firm (Vispero) which tried to dominate the software accessibility market and jacked up the prices to annual subscriptions. He's a electrical engineer so he was comfortable switching to free software NVDA, but a lot of people paid up.

Now with LLM's that business model is in shambles and the finance side of it is less attractive with interest rates so high. I suspect that this is actually driving the software engineer hiring slow-down, because these companies were actually doing most of the employing of software engineers, much more than the big tech companies.

I'm not a SWE, (I'm a data engineer) but this jives with what I saw while looking for work. I'm not a particularly good DE, so I was out there for 18 months. There were still plenty of listings but not many of them were in "tech" companies in the traditional sense. Part of this was leaving a tech hub for what is very much not one, but the biggest issue that I found in landing work was that I was now competing for relatively boring $100k+ jobs with guys who were working $200k+ jobs in 2020 - 2023. The 3 - 6 "tech" orgs that used to employ these folks regionally just aren't really hiring that much.

Yes. I got laid off from Capital One at 3 years of experience in 2025 and I found myself either competing with laid off Amazon employees with 4+ years of experience or applying to junior roles and competing with new grads.

I ended up sidestepping the whole market and now I make $75k NZD, so I'm not sure who won in the end.

The best managers I’ve ever known were some guys who came over to Amazon from Capital One. They were deeply embedded into the EC2 infrastructure systems, including the team I was on — EC2-Chronos. We were responsible for managing all NTP time sync across all of Amazon and AWS, in every single region, availability zone, and datacenter. That includes the isolated and classified regions.

That was also one of the best teams of technical people I’ve ever known.

Sadly, there was also the Amazon and AWS S-Team leadership, who came up with things like RTO and mandatory co-location with your manager. They lost a lot of good people, and I think that was entirely intentional.

I was thinking we should have our own internal saas-pocalypse where I work, or at least threaten one to our vendors.

It used to be that vendors could tie their cost to the value they provide, but now their cost is more correlated to the token spend to reverse engineer and re-implement them (using appropriate clean room controls etc). If their cost goes to far above the AI-driven re-write, they're more likely to get jettisoned (absent some other moat not included purely in the technology).

I'm sure we can all think of products that charge a fair whack in license fees, but would not be massively difficult to re-implement (or at least for the subset of features actually used).

On some level, yes, though when I choose a saas product, what I'm really choosing is not a basket of features, but rather someone else to be worrying about scaling, monitoring, security patches, uptime, etc.

Like in theory your agents can build all that too, but all the ancillary bits benefit a lot from being spread across a pool of users with different time zones, release cycles, whatever.

Exactly, just because you can vibe code an HTML sanitizer or an operation system, doesn't mean that you should..

And its the same reason you'd rather have a SaaS vendor, than asking an agent why the cloud bill keeps climbing and then have to debate the impact of delete such and such VMs or databases that nobody knows what do :)

You also don't ask your agent to start from assembly.

Things you can get upfront as libraries or services are things you and your agent don't have to worry about.

I'm not even sure there is anything new here, just that we have a capability jump with LLMs, you'll probably prefer spending it on building features, not replacing vendors (unless they are crazy expensive).

So I wonder if the more generic SAAS platforms (like Azure, AWS) that can offer scaling, monitoring, security patches, etc. will start to niche or industry specific Saas tools. Since the "basket of features" is not what is really needed.

Yeah, and admittedly you need to pick your problem domain sensibly.

i.e. you wouldn't vibe code your general ledger, but I'd guess Confluence is pretty vulnerable.

Many organizations just want to diffuse responsibility away from themselves and will gladly sign a contract to do so. Paying a vendor is infinitely more affordable than the risk of trying to bring a vendors' core competency in-house.

I think the SaaS-pocalypse is going to surface more from new AI-first SaaS companies entering the market and undercutting incumbents in a way that's difficult to compete with.

At the same time we have to value domain experience when it is a cornerstone. Ive worked for "middleman" companies that at face value seem superfluous only to realize we handled relationships or bureaucracies much more effectively then our clients could and thereby provided concrete value well beyond our cost.

Just use a vendor intelligence service to find out what others are paying to cram down what they're trying to charge you. Lots of competitors in this space, you provide them contract details, they provide a report on how and where to push.

One interesting knock on from the hyperscaler growth we've seen is that the Mag7 have issued so much debt that they are crowding out other companies who would otherwise have no trouble issuing debt.

The private equity and private credit crowd is one of these groups that are currently running into this issue.

There is no way a growing company($15M to $500M in yearly sales is the sweet spot for these private credit companies) can compete with Google on debt terms so they have to raise their rates to compete suddenly, not because of all rates rising but strictly because we've just seen a huge debt issuance from some very solid credit companies.

We haven't seen a shock like this in 20+ years I've followed the credit market where a small group of companies issue so much high quality debt in such a short period of time, note there is also a lot of less high quality debt issued in this same time:)

So much has been issued that credit funds have run out of appetite to acquire Lowe middle market debt at their current spreads. This is just the way markets work so no one is crying in the casino but it is a big shock to the credit markets.

heck there was concern that the US government may have trouble issuing 5-10Y debt at rates they are used to because of the amount of GOOG, META,etc debt that is available at better terms.

Its a wrinkle to the markets that no one really predicted as a knock on effect of AI's growth.

This is all the back drop for BDC(Business Development Companies) and other private credit issuers who normally loan money for 5-7 year terms.

Those cheap 2021 loans to these small private companies are now coming due into this market with the additional head wind that the largest single sector that issued debt was venture backed software companies, who now face the head winds of the macro factors described above and the additional factor of AI commoditizing alot of hte software that these companies are building.

Private credit and equity are going to have a rough couple of years.

Things to watch out for are lack of IPO's and exist from venture/PE backed companies and a proliferation of continuation funds that kick the can down the road.

On the plus side, its a great time to be a credit trader, but not necessarily a credit issuer:)

So traditional Venture firms are not part of this (1). VC buys equity in their start-ups, not debt, so interest rates aren't a direct concern of theirs. And VC firms generally do not borrow, they raise investment funds of investors money and because it is high risk, generally speaking no one lends money to these funds.

Private Equity firms on the other hand do generally take on a lot of debt- they have their own money but they borrow even more (2) and use that amount of money to buy out the current owners of a company. Basically they borrow to turn a steady stream of revenue into the future (an existing software company that is profitable) into a big pile of cash today for the current owners. And then they need to pay off that borrowing over time, from the steady stream of revenue that the software company generates. And if they are wrong about the size of the steady stream of revenue, they basically declare bankruptcy and the people who loaned the money (banks but also pension firms etc.) now run the company.

1: The way that VC changes is that the rising interest rates mean that the returns to safe investments are higher, so in order to attract new capital VC firms have to promise even higher returns as well.

2: They borrow money to get higher returns- if you have 5 dollars in a stock and it goes up 20% you have 6 dollars. If you have 5 dollars and borrow 5 dollars and invest it in a stock that goes up 20% you have 7 dollars after you pay back the loan. The catch is, if the stock instead goes down by 20%, after you pay back the loan you only have 3 dollars. (And if the stock goes down 50% you are wiped out.) But PE firms are confident that their investments will always be winners, so they take out loans like that.

There is some variety, but a very common model in Private Equity is to acquire an asset (a company), and fund that acquisition through either equity or debt.

The ability to purchase often comes in through either Private fund investments or via Debt.

* Private funds are most often drawdown funds (Private equity funds, VC Funds, Real Estate Funds, etc.). These are managed funds not available on public markets, typically require a substantial commitment of funds, and generally in return these investors can expect a significant return on their capital.

* Debt was a very popular way to finance these purchases as well when interests rate were lower, and you expect to sell the asset/company before the debt comes due. Basically cheap money made this feasible/possible.

The expectations are typically 5-10 years for both of these funding models; with private funds, they expect to run for X years, long enough to acquire the assets, clean them up, and resell them at a profit. For debt, the expectation was to sell before the debt came due, along the same timeline.

So that's the backdrop.

Private Equity for Pension Plans? Evaluating Private Equity Performance from an Investor’s Perspective - https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2025/02/03/private-equity-fo... - February 3rd, 2025

- Public pension plans, like many other institutional investors, have steadily increased their allocation to private equity investments over the last two decades. (Figure 1) This trend prompts an important question: do these investments enhance the investment opportunity set by delivering positive risk-adjusted returns, or are they merely high-cost vehicles for taking on risks similar to those available in public markets? In the paper “Private Equity for Pension Plans? Evaluating Private Equity Performance from an Investor’s Perspective” we propose a new methodology to disentangle whether the rates of return associated with private equity (PE) investments represent meaningful outperformance, or just compensation for the risk embedded in these investments. We then apply the methodology to evaluate the returns obtained by public pension plans.

- Our findings suggest that PE financed buyout strategies exhibit modest risk-adjusted outperformance, whereas venture capital and real estate funds do not. We also find that public pension plans tend to perform better in their private equity investments than other private equity investors, but this is mostly due to better access to private equity investments rather than selection ability. Finally, we identify a material correlation between a pension plan’s underfunding and the internal rate of return (IRR) of their private-equity investments; however, this correlation is driven by the fact that underfunded pension plans appear to be choosing comparatively riskier private equity investments, which command higher risk premiums.

Key takeaways:

- Risk-Adjusted Performance: For our sample period, our outperformance measure is approximately zero, indicating that the representative pension plan would not have benefited from changing its allocation to PE. A notable exception is buyout funds, which show a positive risk-adjusted performance. This performance is partly, but not entirely, due to their value exposure. By contrast, VC funds underperformed on average (but less so than publicly traded small-growth firms).

- Selection vs Access: We do not find evidence that pension plans had market timing skill. We do find that the PE funds that were selected by public pension plans outperform the average PE fund of the same vintage year, but this does not seem to be due to a genuine ability to select the better-performing PE investments. Rather, it appears that the PE funds give certain investors preferential access to the better PE investments: pension plan “selectivity skill” disappears when we confine attention to the universe of private equity investments that are continuations of ongoing relationships with a given pension plan, or when we consider first time funds (which are likely to be less selective about their clients).

- Risk-Taking Behavior: We find that underfunded pension plans, and plans with boards that have a larger fraction of state officials and members of the public appointed by a government official, take more risk but earn lower risk-adjusted returns in their PE investments. Investments in PE funds that are located in the pension plan’s state do not differ from out-of-state funds in their level of risk, but they do earn lower risk-adjusted returns. Taken together, these results are suggestive of agency problems, such as gambling for resurrection and political influence, playing an important role in the selection of PE investments by pension plans.
